outline.title: Adolescent Health Medicine: Five Foundations
outline.logline: In three minutes, a hook-to-recap tour of adolescent health medicine: what it is, how adolescents develop, how to talk with them, and the law that guards them.

scenes.title: What Adolescent Health Is
scenes.summary: Defines adolescent health as the physical, psychological and social well-being of people aged 10 to 19, and fixes the age bands adolescents, youth and young people.
scenes.teach: Why does a ten to nineteen year old need their own branch of medicine? Adolescent health is the physical, psychological and social well-being of people aged 10 to 19. Picture a phone with three bars: body, mind and social life, each needing signal. The World Health Organization calls ages 10 to 19 adolescents, 15 to 24 youth, and 10 to 24 young people. Health here is well-being, not merely the absence of disease. So the work is prevention, early intervention and promotion of healthy behaviours, not just treating illness.
points: Definition: adolescent health is physical, psychological and social well-being, ages 10 to 19 — show the biopsychosocial triangle, sides labelled Physical, Mental/Emotional, Social, with 'well-being, not just no disease' inside.

Age bands: adolescents 10 to 19, youth 15 to 24, young people 10 to 24 — show the adolescent timeline, a line from 10 to 19 with three coloured bands, a bracket 15 to 24 labelled youth and a bracket 10 to 24 labelled young people.
Scope of work: prevention, early intervention, promotion of healthy behaviours — show three icons in a row: a shield, a clock, a heart.

scenes.title: Four Domains of Development
scenes.summary: Teaches the four domains of adolescent development, physical, cognitive, emotional and social, with puberty and Tanner staging, abstract thinking, mood swings, identity and peer influence.
scenes.teach: Adolescent development moves in four domains at the same time: physical, cognitive, emotional and social. Physically, puberty begins, and Tanner staging tracks the growth spurt and the new secondary sexual characteristics. Cognitively, abstract thinking arrives, so problem-solving and decision-making improve. Emotionally, self-awareness rises, mood swings come and go, and the search for identity runs underneath. Socially, peer relationships strengthen, independence is wanted, and social media shapes the day. Four engines, one car: if one stalls, the whole ride shakes. Each runs on its own clock.
points: Physical domain: onset of puberty, Tanner staging, growth spurts, secondary sexual characteristics — show the five domain cards, the Puberty card lit with a hormones and body-change icon.
Cognitive domain: abstract thinking, problem-solving, decision-making — light the Cognition card, icon 'abstract thinking'.
Emotional and identity: self-awareness, mood swings, search for identity — light the Emotion card (mood regulation) and the Identity card (sense of self).
Social domain: peer relationships, independence, social media influence — light the Social card, icon 'peer belonging'.

scenes.title: Risks and Protective Factors
scenes.summary: Teaches the main risk-taking behaviours of adolescence, substance use, unprotected sex and violence, and the protective factors of parental support, education and positive peer influence.
scenes.teach: Risk-taking rises because impulse control is still maturing. Substance use begins as experimentation with alcohol, tobacco or drugs, driven by peer pressure or curiosity. Unprotected sex raises the risk of STIs, teenage pregnancy and emotional stress. Violence, bullying and gang activity grow from poor impulse control or a harsh environment. Protective factors act like brakes: parental support and open communication, school engagement and health education, and positive peer influence, where friends with healthy habits reinforce good decisions. Brakes beat horns.
points: Substance use: experimentation with alcohol, tobacco or drugs from peer pressure or curiosity — show a risk card with two arrows labelled 'peer pressure' and 'curiosity'.
Unprotected sex: higher risk of STIs, teenage pregnancy and emotional stress — show a second risk card.
Violence: fights, bullying, gang activity from poor impulse control or environmental factors — show a third risk card with an environment arrow.
Protective factors: parental support, education, positive peer influence — show three brake icons pressing back on the three risk cards.

scenes.title: Three Stages, Three Tasks
scenes.summary: Teaches the three stages of adolescence, early 10 to 13, middle 14 to 17 and late 18 to 19, with each stage's task, then checks the learner with a 15-year-old case.
scenes.teach: Adolescence has three stages, and each one asks a different question. In early adolescence, ages 10 to 13, puberty begins and body image worries appear. In middle adolescence, 14 to 17, identity is explored and emotions fluctuate widely. In late adolescence, 18 to 19, independence grows and career focus takes over. Here is a check: a 15-year-old worries about how she looks to her friends. Which stage, and which task, is she in?
points: Early adolescence, 10 to 13: puberty onset and body image issues — highlight the first band of the timeline.
Middle adolescence, 14 to 17: identity exploration and emotional fluctuation — highlight the middle band.
Late adolescence, 18 to 19: greater independence and career focus — highlight the last band.
Check question: a 15-year-old worried about her friends' opinion is in middle adolescence, exploring identity — freeze the timeline on the middle band.

scenes.title: Talking So They Tell You
scenes.summary: Teaches a confidential, respectful and non-judgemental approach with shared decision-making, then the HEADSSS psychosocial history.
scenes.teach: That 15-year-old was in middle adolescence, exploring identity. Now communication. Be confidential, respectful and non-judgemental: adolescents open up when they feel safe and trusted. Assure confidentiality, avoid criticism and moral judgement, and the rapport brings honest answers. Use shared decision-making: explain the options clearly, let them state preferences, and autonomy, adherence and trust all rise. Then take the HEADSSS history: Home, Education or Employment, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide or Depression, and Safety. One interview, seven windows. Ask, do not lecture.
points: Confidential, respectful, non-judgemental approach builds rapport and honest communication — show the communication cycle with the lock icon labelled confidentiality and two figures, clinician and adolescent.
Shared decision-making: explain options, hear preferences; it promotes autonomy, adherence and trust — show the 'Plan together' arrow on the cycle.
HEADSSS psychosocial assessment: Home, Education/Employment, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/Depression, Safety — show the vertical HEADSSS checklist, each letter with its icon, words exact.

scenes.title: Law, Consent and Recap
scenes.summary: Teaches the Child Rights Act 2003, the National Policy on Adolescent Health 2007 and how consent laws vary by region, then recaps the episode's key term.
scenes.teach: Law shapes what you may do. Nigeria's Child Rights Act of 2003 protects minors from abuse and exploitation. The National Policy on Adolescent Health of 2007 covers reproductive health, education and empowerment. Consent laws vary by region, and they matter most in HIV testing, contraceptives and mental health. Assent, parental permission, the mature minor and the limits of confidentiality all hinge on age thresholds. Recap: adolescent health is the well-being of 10- to 19-year-olds, and the law sets who may consent.

beats.say: Risk-taking rises because impulse control is still maturing.
Substance use begins as experimentation with alcohol, tobacco or drugs.
Peer pressure or curiosity drives it.
Unprotected sex raises the risk of STIs, teenage pregnancy and emotional stress.
Violence, bullying and gang activity grow from poor impulse control.
A harsh environment can drive it too.
Protective factors act like brakes.
Parental support and open communication are the first.
School engagement and health education promote informed choices.
Positive peer influence means friends with healthy habits reinforce good decisions.
Brakes beat horns.

beats.say: That 15-year-old was in middle adolescence, exploring identity.
Now, communication.
Be confidential, respectful and non-judgemental; adolescents open up when they feel safe and trusted.
Assure confidentiality, avoid criticism and moral judgement, and the rapport brings honest answers.
Use shared decision-making: explain the options clearly, let them state preferences, and autonomy, adherence and trust all rise.
Then take the HEADSSS history: Home, Education or Employment, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide or Depression, and Safety.
One interview, seven windows.
Ask, do not lecture.

cast.brief: A vertical checklist with seven rows. The words 'Home', 'Education or Employment', 'Activities', 'Drugs', 'Sexuality', 'Suicide or Depression', 'Safety' are written exactly beside each letter.
cast.motion: The rows appear one by one from top to bottom as the voice names each letter; a gentle highlight moves down the list.

cast.name: Confidentiality

cast.motion: The padlock gently pulses, and a soft glow appears around it when confidentiality is mentioned.

beats.say: Law shapes what you may do.
Nigeria's Child Rights Act of 2003 protects minors from abuse and exploitation.
The National Policy on Adolescent Health of 2007 covers reproductive health, education and empowerment.
Consent laws vary by region, and they matter most in HIV testing, contraceptives and mental health.
Assent, parental permission, the mature minor and the limits of confidentiality all hinge on age thresholds.
So adolescent health is the well-being of 10- to 19-year-olds, and the law sets who may consent.

cast.name: Child Rights Act 2003
cast.brief: A wooden judge's gavel, side view, resting on a round sound block. The handle points right. Simple brown wood, with a small blank label plate on the block (no text). No people.
cast.motion: The gavel lifts slightly and taps down once.

cast.name: National Policy 2007
cast.brief: A single page of a government policy document, slightly tilted. The page has a bold title 'National Policy on Adolescent Health 2007' and a small emblem. A pen lies beside it. No people, no extra text.
cast.motion: The page settles gently, as if just placed down.

cast.name: Consent and confidentiality ladder
cast.brief: A five-rung ladder, side view, with rungs labelled from bottom to top: 'Minor', 'Assent', 'Parental consent', 'Mature minor', 'Confidentiality limits'. A small gavel icon sits beside the top rung, and a sign at the bottom reads 'mandatory reporting: abuse, risk of harm'. No people.
cast.motion: Each rung glows in turn from bottom to top.

cast.name: Adolescent health timeline
cast.brief: A horizontal line from 10 to 19 with three coloured bands: early adolescence 10–13, middle 14–16, late 17–19. Below, a bracket 15–24 labelled youth, and 10–24 labelled young people. No people.
cast.motion: The bands fill in one by one from left to right.
